stem: Before training a loan model, a data science team wants to measure whether its training data under-represents certain age groups or has very different approval labels across groups.
prompt: Which AWS capability is designed for this?

options.text: SageMaker Clarify post-training bias metrics
options.why: Post-training metrics analyze a trained model's predictions; the team wants to check the data before training.

options.text: SageMaker Model Monitor bias drift monitoring
options.why: Bias drift monitoring watches a deployed model over time; no model exists yet.

options.text: SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias analysis
options.why: Clarify's pre-training metrics, such as class imbalance and differences in label proportions, measure bias in the dataset before training.

options.text: Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery
options.why: Macie finds sensitive data in S3; it does not measure representation or label differences across groups.

explanation.answer: Amazon SageMaker Clarify detects potential bias in data before training (pre-training metrics such as class imbalance and difference in positive proportions in labels) and in model predictions after training, and explains predictions with feature attributions.
explanation.concept: Detecting bias early in data is cheaper than fixing a biased model after deployment.
explanation.examTip: Measure bias in data or predictions = SageMaker Clarify.

stem: A trained hiring model is about to be deployed. The team wants to check whether its predictions have different accuracy or approval rates across demographic groups.
prompt: Which approach should the team use?

options.text: Compare overall accuracy with the previous model
options.why: Overall accuracy can hide large differences between groups.

options.text: Run pre-training bias metrics on the training data
options.why: Data metrics show imbalance in the dataset, not whether the trained model's predictions differ by group.

options.text: Manually review a few predictions for each group
options.why: A handful of examples cannot reliably reveal systematic differences in accuracy or approval rates.

options.text: Clarify post-training bias metrics and subgroup analysis
options.why: Post-training bias analysis compares prediction outcomes and error rates across groups before deployment.

explanation.answer: Subgroup analysis evaluates model performance and outcomes separately for different groups. SageMaker Clarify provides post-training bias metrics (such as differences in positive prediction rates or accuracy between groups) to identify unfair predictions.
explanation.concept: Fairness evaluation should happen before deployment and continuously afterward, because bias can drift.
explanation.examTip: Overall metrics can hide group gaps → subgroup analysis.

stem: A credit model passed fairness checks at launch. A year later, the applicant population has changed, and the team suspects outcomes may have become less fair.
prompt: Which capability monitors for this automatically in production?

options.text: Model Monitor bias drift monitoring with Clarify metrics
options.why: Model Monitor can track bias metrics on live predictions over time and alert when they drift beyond thresholds.

options.text: Model Monitor data quality monitoring on the endpoint
options.why: Data quality monitoring tracks statistical changes in inputs, not whether outcomes have become less fair across groups.

options.text: A one-time Clarify bias report run each year
options.why: Annual reports leave long gaps; the requirement is automatic monitoring in production.

options.text: CloudWatch alarms on the endpoint's error rate
options.why: Error rates show technical failures, not unfair outcomes.

explanation.answer: Bias can drift after deployment as data changes. SageMaker Model Monitor integrates with SageMaker Clarify to monitor bias drift and feature attribution drift on endpoints, alerting through Amazon CloudWatch when metrics exceed thresholds.
explanation.concept: Responsible AI requires continuous monitoring, not one-time checks.
explanation.examTip: Fairness changes after launch = bias drift → Model Monitor + Clarify.

references.title: Data and model quality monitoring with Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor

stem: A team building a skin-condition image classifier notices that 90% of its training images are of light skin tones.
prompt: Which dataset characteristic should the team improve?

options.text: Higher image resolution so lesions are clearer
options.why: Sharper images do not fix the model's lack of exposure to darker skin tones.

options.text: Diversity and balance across skin tones
options.why: With 90% light skin tones, the model will perform worse for others; balanced, diverse data fixes the gap.

options.text: Label consistency between annotators
options.why: Nothing suggests labels are inconsistent; the problem is who is represented in the data.

options.text: Total dataset size, by adding more images of any kind
options.why: Adding more images of the same mix keeps the imbalance.

explanation.answer: Responsible datasets are inclusive, diverse, curated and balanced, covering the populations and conditions the model will encounter. Under-representation leads to higher error rates for those groups.
explanation.concept: Remedies include collecting more data for under-represented groups, careful resampling, and evaluating performance per group.
explanation.examTip: One group dominates the data → improve diversity and balance.

stem: A company plans to train a customer-service model using text scraped from random internet forums, including posts full of offensive language and misinformation.
prompt: Which responsible dataset practice is MOST important?

options.text: Use the full scrape and filter outputs with guardrails
options.why: Guardrails catch some outputs, but a model trained on toxic and false text will keep producing it.

options.text: Use only the most recent forum posts
options.why: Recent posts can be just as toxic and inaccurate; recency is not curation.

options.text: Use curated, trustworthy sources and filter toxic content
options.why: Models reproduce what they learn, so curated, high-quality sources reduce toxic and false outputs.

options.text: Use the full scrape but train for fewer epochs
options.why: Training less does not stop the model learning harmful patterns from the data.

explanation.answer: Curated data sources, with known provenance, appropriate licensing and quality controls, are a key characteristic of responsible datasets. Filtering toxic or false content and documenting sources reduces harmful model behavior.
explanation.concept: Data lineage and cataloging (Domain 5) support knowing where training data came from.
explanation.examTip: Responsible datasets are curated, not random scrapes.

stem: A model's predictions change dramatically when it is retrained on slightly different samples of the same data, and it performs much better on training data than on new data.
prompt: Which problem does this indicate?

options.text: High bias (underfitting)
options.why: Underfit models perform poorly even on training data; this model does very well on it.

options.text: Data drift in production
options.why: Drift is a change in data after deployment; here instability appears just from retraining on similar samples.

options.text: Class imbalance in the labels
options.why: Imbalance does not explain predictions swinging between retraining runs.

options.text: High variance (overfitting)
options.why: High variance means sensitivity to the specific training sample, shown as unstable models and a training-versus-new-data gap.

explanation.answer: Variance is error from sensitivity to small fluctuations in training data. High-variance models overfit: they fit training data closely and generalize poorly. Bias is error from overly simple assumptions, leading to underfitting.
explanation.concept: Effects of bias and variance include inaccuracy, overfitting, underfitting and uneven effects on demographic groups (for example a model that overfits to majority groups).
explanation.examTip: Unstable + great on train, poor on new = high variance (overfitting).

stem: A speech model trained mostly on one dialect has low error for that dialect but high error for others. Adding more data from the dominant dialect does not help the other dialects.
prompt: Which explanation and remedy are MOST appropriate?

options.text: Other dialects are under-represented; add their data, test by group
options.why: Performance gaps across groups come from unrepresentative data; targeted data collection and per-group evaluation address them.

options.text: The model is too small; switch to a larger model architecture
options.why: A larger model trained on the same skewed data would still underperform for the other dialects.

options.text: The labels are inconsistent; retrain the annotators first
options.why: Nothing points to labeling problems; the gap follows which dialects are in the data.

options.text: The model is overfitting; add stronger regularization
options.why: Regularization reduces overfitting in general but does not supply the missing dialect data.

explanation.answer: Bias in data affects demographic groups unequally: models perform best for groups well represented in training. Remedies include collecting representative data, rebalancing, and measuring performance per subgroup.
explanation.concept: Inclusivity and fairness depend on dataset representativeness, not just dataset size.
explanation.examTip: Group-specific errors → representative data for that group + subgroup evaluation.

stem: A content moderation model flags posts in one dialect as toxic far more often than equivalent posts in standard English. Investigation finds that human labelers marked many harmless dialect posts as toxic.
prompt: Which bias detection practice found the root cause?

options.text: Increasing inference throughput
options.why: Throughput does not reveal labeling problems.

options.text: Analyzing label quality
options.why: Reviewing how examples were labeled revealed that biased labels taught the model to over-flag the dialect.

options.text: Prompt caching
options.why: Prompt caching reduces cost for repeated prompts and has nothing to do with how training data was labeled.

options.text: Changing embedding dimensions
options.why: Embedding size does not expose biased labels.

explanation.answer: Label quality analysis checks whether training labels are accurate and consistent across groups. Biased or inconsistent human labels are a common source of model bias.
explanation.concept: Other bias and trustworthiness detection methods in the exam guide: human audits and subgroup analysis.
explanation.examTip: Model bias traced to how data was labeled = label quality analysis.

stem: A public-sector agency uses an ML model to prioritize benefit applications for caseworkers. Each quarter, it wants independent experts to look back at a sample of past decisions and judge whether they were fair and correct. The review must not delay any individual application.
prompt: Which practice meets these requirements?

options.text: Periodic human audits of a sample of past decisions
options.why: A human audit has qualified reviewers examine a sample of completed decisions after the fact, which matches the quarterly, independent, look-back review and adds no delay to live applications.

options.text: Amazon Augmented AI reviews of low-confidence predictions
options.why: Amazon A2I sends individual predictions to reviewers before they are used, which adds a step to live applications. It also covers only low-confidence cases, not a fairness review of a sample of all decisions.

options.text: SageMaker Clarify bias metrics on the training data
options.why: Pre-training bias metrics measure imbalance in the dataset before the model is built. They do not involve independent experts judging real decisions the model has already made.

options.text: Bias drift monitoring with SageMaker Model Monitor
options.why: Bias drift monitoring is automated and tracks statistical metrics over time. It is useful, but it is not experts judging whether specific decisions were fair and correct.

explanation.answer: Human audits are periodic reviews in which qualified, ideally independent, people examine samples of AI decisions for fairness, accuracy and compliance. They complement automated metrics and do not change the live decision flow.
explanation.concept: Tell the human-oversight options apart by timing: Amazon A2I reviews individual predictions before they are acted on; human audits review a sample of decisions afterward; Clarify and Model Monitor provide automated metrics.
explanation.examTip: "Experts periodically review a sample of past decisions" = human audit. "Route low-confidence predictions to a person before acting" = Amazon A2I.

references.title: Using Amazon Augmented AI for human review

stem: A responsible AI team assembles methods to detect and monitor bias, trustworthiness and truthfulness.
prompt: Which methods should it include? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Removing all monitoring after launch
options.why: Bias can drift, so monitoring must continue after launch.

options.text: Analyzing label quality in training data
options.why: Biased or inconsistent labels are a major source of model bias.

options.text: Measuring only average latency
options.why: Latency does not reveal bias or truthfulness issues.

options.text: Subgroup analysis of performance and outcomes
options.why: Comparing results across groups reveals disparities hidden by overall metrics.

options.text: Human audits of sampled decisions
options.why: Expert review catches issues automated metrics miss.

explanation.answer: Tools and practices to detect and monitor bias, trustworthiness and truthfulness include analyzing label quality, human audits, subgroup analysis, automated bias metrics (SageMaker Clarify), bias drift monitoring (Model Monitor) and evaluation of generative outputs for toxicity and accuracy.
explanation.concept: Combine automated metrics with human judgment for robust oversight.
explanation.examTip: Label quality + human audits + subgroup analysis.

references.title: Data and model quality monitoring with Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor

stem: A team removed the race attribute from a lending dataset to avoid bias. Analysis shows the model still produces disparate outcomes across racial groups, largely driven by the applicant's postal code.
prompt: What is the MOST likely explanation?

options.text: The model has too few parameters to be fair
options.why: Model size does not explain disparities driven by one specific feature.

options.text: Race data is still leaking through a hidden column
options.why: The analysis shows the disparity is driven by postal code, not by a leftover race column.

options.text: The model is overfitting to rare postal codes
options.why: Overfitting would add noise, not a systematic pattern across racial groups.

options.text: Postal code acts as a proxy for race
options.why: Features correlated with a protected attribute can reintroduce bias even after the attribute itself is removed.

explanation.answer: Proxy variables are features correlated with protected attributes (for example postal code with race). Removing the protected attribute is not enough; teams must measure outcomes across groups and examine feature influence to detect proxy bias.
explanation.concept: SageMaker Clarify feature attributions help reveal which features drive predictions, aiding proxy detection.
explanation.examTip: Removed sensitive attribute but bias remains → look for proxy features.

stem: A team considers pre-training its own large language model from scratch for a common summarization use case that existing models already handle well.
prompt: From a sustainability perspective, what is the BEST recommendation?

options.text: Use an existing model, adapted with prompts, RAG or light tuning
options.why: Reusing a pre-trained model avoids the very large energy footprint of pre-training.

options.text: Pre-train a smaller model, since smaller uses less energy
options.why: Even a small model's pre-training costs far more energy than reusing an existing model that already does the job.

options.text: Pre-train in a Region powered by renewable energy
options.why: Cleaner energy helps, but avoiding unnecessary pre-training saves far more.

options.text: Fine-tune the largest available model for the task
options.why: An oversized model uses more energy for every request than the task needs.

explanation.answer: Responsible model selection includes environmental considerations. Reusing pre-trained models, choosing appropriately sized models, using efficient hardware and avoiding unnecessary training reduce energy consumption and carbon footprint.
explanation.concept: The AWS Well-Architected sustainability guidance encourages using managed services and right-sizing resources.
explanation.examTip: Sustainability: reuse pre-trained models, right-size, avoid needless training.

stem: A team reviews its training dataset against responsible AI guidelines.
prompt: Which characteristics should a responsible dataset have? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Unknown origin and licensing
options.why: Responsible data has known provenance and appropriate rights.

options.text: Balanced representation so that no relevant group is severely under-represented
options.why: Balance reduces systematic errors for minority groups.

options.text: Inclusive and diverse coverage of the people and scenarios the model will serve
options.why: Diverse, inclusive data helps the model perform well for all users.

options.text: Data collected only from the development team's own devices
options.why: A narrow source is unlikely to represent real users.

options.text: As many duplicate records as possible
options.why: Duplicates skew the data and add no new information.

explanation.answer: Characteristics of responsible datasets include inclusivity, diversity, curated data sources and balanced representation, along with accurate labels, appropriate consent and licensing, and documented lineage.
explanation.concept: Dataset quality and representativeness are the foundation for fair and robust models.
explanation.examTip: Inclusive, diverse, curated, balanced.

stem: A team wants to test whether its generative AI job-description writer produces different language quality or stereotypes depending on the gender implied in prompts.
prompt: Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Run a toxicity evaluation on a large, varied set of prompts
options.why: Toxicity scores catch offensive content, not subtler differences in quality or stereotypes between groups.

options.text: Paired prompts differing only in implied gender, then compare
options.why: Controlled paired prompts isolate the effect of gender, and automated metrics plus human review reveal differences.

options.text: Check the provider's published bias benchmark
options.why: A general benchmark does not test this specific job-description use case.

options.text: Ask the model whether its descriptions are biased
options.why: A model's self-assessment is not reliable evidence of its own bias.

explanation.answer: Bias in generative models can be tested with counterfactual or paired prompts that vary only a sensitive attribute, comparing outputs for sentiment, quality, stereotypes and refusals. Automated evaluations (including LLM-as-a-judge) and human reviewers assess differences.
explanation.concept: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation and SageMaker Clarify foundation model evaluations include bias and stereotyping assessments.
explanation.examTip: Test GenAI bias with prompts that differ only in the sensitive attribute.

references.title: Evaluate the performance of Amazon Bedrock resources

stem: A very simple model predicts insurance claim amounts poorly for every group of customers, on both training and new data.
prompt: Which statement describes the problem?

options.text: High variance (overfitting) to the training data
options.why: Overfitting shows good training performance and poor new-data performance, not poor performance everywhere.

options.text: Data drift since training
options.why: The model is poor even on its training data, so drift is not the cause.

options.text: High bias (underfitting): the model is too simple
options.why: Poor results everywhere, including on training data, indicate the model is too simple to capture the patterns.

options.text: Class imbalance across the customer groups
options.why: Imbalance would hurt some groups more than others; here every group is predicted poorly.

explanation.answer: High bias causes underfitting: the model is too simple, so it is inaccurate on training and new data alike. Increasing model capacity or adding informative features helps.
explanation.concept: The bias-variance trade-off: reduce bias with more capacity, reduce variance with more data, regularization or simpler models.
explanation.examTip: Bad everywhere = high bias / underfitting.

stem: A company wants to use recordings of customer support calls to train a speech model. The original privacy notice said recordings were for quality assurance only.
prompt: What should the company do before using the recordings for training?

options.text: Encrypt the recordings before using them for training
options.why: Encryption protects the data but does not provide a legal basis for the new purpose.

options.text: Use them, since quality assurance covers model training
options.why: Training a model is a new purpose beyond what customers were told.

options.text: Use them once customer names are removed
options.why: De-identification helps, but the company still needs a legal basis or consent for the new purpose.

options.text: Confirm a legal basis or consent, and de-identify personal data
options.why: Using data beyond its stated purpose requires a legal basis or consent, and minimizing personal data reduces privacy risk.

explanation.answer: Responsible datasets respect privacy: data should be used only for purposes with a valid legal basis or consent, minimized, and de-identified where possible. Purpose limitation is a core privacy principle.
explanation.concept: Data governance (Domain 5) covers lifecycles, retention and documented usage of data.
explanation.examTip: New use of personal data → check consent/legal basis + de-identify.

stem: An ML team on SageMaker AI wants to evaluate a foundation model it hosts for issues such as stereotyping, toxicity and factual knowledge before deployment.
prompt: Which capability supports this?

options.text: SageMaker AI foundation model evaluations (Clarify)
options.why: SageMaker AI evaluates foundation models for dimensions such as stereotyping, toxicity, factual knowledge and robustness.

options.text: SageMaker Model Monitor on the production endpoint
options.why: Model Monitor tracks drift in production; it does not run pre-deployment stereotyping and knowledge evaluations.

options.text: SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias metrics
options.why: Pre-training metrics analyze tabular training datasets, not a foundation model's generated text.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails content filters
options.why: Guardrails filter content at runtime; they do not evaluate a model before deployment.

explanation.answer: SageMaker AI offers foundation model evaluations (built on SageMaker Clarify) that assess models for quality and responsibility dimensions such as factual knowledge, toxicity, prompt stereotyping and semantic robustness, with automatic and human evaluation options.
explanation.concept: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation offers similar capabilities for models used through Bedrock.
explanation.examTip: Evaluate an FM for stereotyping/toxicity on SageMaker = FM evaluations (Clarify).

references.title: Evaluate the performance of Amazon Bedrock resources

stem: A medical model is very accurate for the patient groups that make up most of its training data but makes erratic predictions for a small patient group with few examples.
prompt: Which statement BEST describes this situation?

options.text: The model is fair, because its overall accuracy is high
options.why: High overall accuracy can hide poor performance for small groups.

options.text: Sparse data for the small group makes its predictions unreliable
options.why: Groups with little data get less accurate, less stable predictions, an effect of bias and variance on demographic groups.

options.text: The small group's records were mislabeled by the annotators
options.why: Nothing points to labeling errors; the group simply has too few examples.

options.text: The model underfits all patient groups equally
options.why: The model is very accurate for most groups, so it is not underfitting.

explanation.answer: Bias and variance can affect demographic groups unequally. Groups with little data often get less accurate and less stable predictions. Subgroup evaluation exposes this; remedies include gathering more data for the group and careful modeling choices.
explanation.concept: Fairness requires examining per-group metrics, not only aggregate accuracy.
explanation.examTip: Small group, erratic predictions → data scarcity for that group, check subgroups.

stem: A company establishes an AI review board, defines policies for acceptable AI use, and requires risk assessments and documentation before any AI system is launched.
prompt: Which responsible AI dimension does this represent?

options.text: Inference
options.why: Inference is using a trained model to make predictions.

options.text: Chunking
options.why: Chunking splits documents for retrieval.

options.text: Governance
options.why: Governance means policies, processes and oversight structures that ensure AI is developed and used responsibly.

options.text: Tokenization
options.why: Tokenization splits text into units for a model. It is not a policy or oversight structure.

explanation.answer: Governance incorporates best practices into the AI supply chain, including policies, roles and responsibilities, review processes, risk assessments, documentation and audits.
explanation.concept: Governance frameworks such as the AWS Generative AI Security Scoping Matrix help classify use cases and apply appropriate controls (Domain 5).
explanation.examTip: Policies, review boards, risk assessments = governance.

stem: In a dataset for predicting loan default, only 2% of examples come from small-business applicants, who are an important customer segment.
prompt: Which risk does this create, and what is a reasonable response?

options.text: Duplicate the segment's records many times
options.why: Duplicating the same few records can cause overfitting to them; new representative data is better.

options.text: No risk, because the overall model is accurate
options.why: Overall accuracy can hide poor performance for a small, important segment.

options.text: Remove the segment so it does not skew the overall model
options.why: Removing it guarantees poor performance for those applicants.

options.text: Risk of poor or unfair results; get more data, evaluate it
options.why: Under-represented segments often see higher error rates, so more data and per-segment evaluation address the risk.

explanation.answer: Imbalanced representation leads to models that underperform for minority segments. Remedies include collecting more data, resampling or weighting, and evaluating each segment with appropriate metrics.
explanation.concept: SageMaker Clarify's class imbalance metric quantifies representation differences in training data.
explanation.examTip: Tiny segment in data → risk of poor/unfair performance for that segment.

stem: A recommendation model shows popular items more often, which makes them more popular, so the model shows them even more. Niche creators' content rarely gets shown, regardless of quality.
prompt: Which bias pattern does this describe?

options.text: A feedback loop that amplifies popularity bias
options.why: The model's own outputs shape future data, reinforcing and amplifying the initial bias toward popular items.

options.text: Historical bias in the original training labels
options.why: The bias grows because of the model's own effect over time, not only because of the starting data.

options.text: Sampling bias from collecting data in one region
options.why: Nothing suggests data came from one region; exposure drives the pattern.

options.text: Proxy bias from a feature linked to creators
options.why: The pattern comes from popularity reinforcing itself, not a feature standing in for a protected attribute.

explanation.answer: Feedback loops occur when model outputs influence the data used for future training, amplifying existing biases. Mitigations include exploration strategies, fairness constraints in ranking, monitoring exposure across groups and periodic human review.
explanation.concept: Bias can emerge after deployment, so continuous monitoring is part of responsible AI.
explanation.examTip: Model output → more data for same items → stronger bias = feedback loop.

stem: A company is choosing a foundation model for a public-facing assistant and wants to select responsibly.
prompt: Which practice reflects responsible model selection?

options.text: Choose the model with the top score on public benchmarks
options.why: Benchmarks show general capability, not fairness, safety or licensing for this use case.

options.text: Check its documentation and license; test fairness and safety
options.why: Responsible selection weighs documented limitations, licensing and evaluations of fairness and safety for the use case.

options.text: Choose the newest model from the largest model provider
options.why: Recency and provider size do not demonstrate suitability or safety.

options.text: Choose the model with the lowest price per token
options.why: Cost matters, but alone it ignores safety, fairness and licensing.

explanation.answer: Responsible model selection includes reviewing model documentation (such as model cards or AWS AI Service Cards), intended uses and limitations, licensing, safety and bias evaluations, environmental impact, and testing on the specific use case.
explanation.concept: Transparency artifacts help organizations choose and use models appropriately (Task 4.2).
explanation.examTip: Responsible selection = documentation + licensing + fairness/safety evaluation + sustainability.

references.title: Evaluate the performance of Amazon Bedrock resources

stem: A team wants to monitor whether its customer-facing generative assistant keeps giving truthful, accurate answers over time as products and policies change.
prompt: Which approach BEST supports this?

options.text: Run a full evaluation once a year
options.why: Products and policies change far more often than yearly checks can catch.

options.text: Track user satisfaction ratings only
options.why: Users may not notice inaccurate answers, so satisfaction alone does not measure truthfulness.

options.text: Regularly check sampled answers against current sources
options.why: Ongoing evaluation against current sources, with grounding checks and human review, shows when truthfulness declines.

options.text: Monitor latency and error rates on the model endpoint
options.why: These are operational metrics; they say nothing about whether answers are true.

explanation.answer: Monitoring trustworthiness and truthfulness requires ongoing evaluation of real outputs: grounding checks against sources, LLM-as-a-judge or rule-based checks, human review of samples, and user feedback, tracked over time.
explanation.concept: Updating knowledge bases promptly and monitoring accuracy keep RAG applications truthful.
explanation.examTip: Truthfulness over time → continuous evaluation of production outputs.

references.title: Evaluate the performance of Amazon Bedrock resources

stem: A company trains a promotion-recommendation model on 20 years of past promotion decisions, during which managers rarely promoted employees who worked part-time.
prompt: What is the MAIN risk?

options.text: It will overfit, because 20 years is too much data
options.why: More data generally helps generalization; the problem is what the labels reflect.

options.text: It will drift as the company grows
options.why: Drift may happen later, but the main risk comes from the historical decisions it learns from.

options.text: It will be hard to explain to managers
options.why: Explainability is a concern, but the main risk is reproducing unfair past decisions.

options.text: It learns and repeats bias against part-time employees
options.why: Training on historically biased decisions teaches the model to reproduce, and scale, that bias.

explanation.answer: Historical bias occurs when training labels reflect past unfair decisions. Models trained on them reproduce and can scale those biases. Teams should examine labels, measure outcomes across groups, and reconsider whether historical decisions are appropriate targets.
explanation.concept: Responsible AI starts with questioning whether the data reflects the outcomes you actually want.
explanation.examTip: Training labels from biased past decisions = historical bias.

stem: An organization wants to reduce the environmental impact of its AI workloads.
prompt: Which practices help? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use energy-efficient, purpose-built hardware such as AWS Inferentia and Trainium where suitable
options.why: Purpose-built accelerators aim for better performance per watt.

options.text: Send every request to multiple models and discard most answers
options.why: Sending each request to several models and discarding most answers wastes compute and energy.

options.text: Use the smallest model that meets quality requirements
options.why: Smaller models need less compute and energy per request.

options.text: Retrain large models from scratch every week regardless of need
options.why: Unnecessary training consumes large amounts of energy.

options.text: Keep idle GPU instances running at all times
options.why: Idle GPU instances consume energy while doing no useful work, increasing environmental impact.

explanation.answer: Sustainable AI practices include right-sizing models, reusing pre-trained models, efficient hardware, serverless or auto-scaling infrastructure to avoid idle capacity, and avoiding unnecessary training runs.
explanation.concept: Environmental considerations are part of responsible model selection in the exam guide.
explanation.examTip: Right-size, reuse, efficient hardware, no idle capacity.
